title: Hosted API onboarding ladder and fallback patterns
summary: Draft PRD exploring a staged developer onboarding "ladder" for Hosted API SDKs and examples of graceful fallback patterns for streaming + tool-calls + structured output. Focus: lower time-to-success for new users while preserving latency SLOs and observability.
body:
Context:
We keep shipping richer streaming semantics, typed tool-calls, and progressive structured outputs. Teams repeatedly tell us that the first 10–30 minutes of a new integration are the most important conversion window: if developers can get a prototype working quickly (even with lower fidelity), they’re far more likely to expand usage.

Problem statement:
- Current SDK examples assume full-featured streaming + tool orchestration + strict structured schemas. That increases friction: more setup (websockets, function adapters, schema definitions), more surface area for bugs.
- When latency spikes or a tool layer fails, the developer experience is opaque; SDKs either bubble raw errors or silently degrade with unexpected JSON.
- Telemetry is present but not surfaced at the sample app level: new users don't know which knob to flip (batching, partial responses, switch to non-streaming) to meet budgets.

Goals (what success looks like):
1) Developer onboarding ladder: provide a sequence of progressively richer integration steps (QuickStart -> Progressive Streaming -> Tool-Enabled Flow -> Schema-Strict Production). Each step should be runnable in <15 minutes with clear success criteria.
2) Fallback primitives: standard SDK-level patterns that automatically downgrade fidelity when latency or tool failures cross thresholds, while preserving clear developer-visible signals.
3) Observability-first examples: sample apps that show token-level latency, tool-call latency, and structured-output validation failures in plain UI/console logs.
4) Minimal config defaults: sensible server-side and SDK defaults so novices succeed without reading long docs.
5) Backwards-compatible: patterns must work with existing hosted endpoints and the typical streaming partial-response contract.

Proposed product components:
A) Onboarding ladder artifacts (deliverables):
- Starter template: single-call, non-streaming example (Node/Python) that returns a simple string output for a prompt. Minimal deps. Success: GET /health + single API call.
- Streaming incremental example: opt-in streaming with an example client that renders partial text frames. Includes a short WebSocket fallback for networks where SSE is blocked. Success: first partial token within 300ms under normal conditions.
- Tool-call sample: lightweight adapter showing 2 local tool stubs (search, calendar) with clear tool handshake example. Shows how to stub in tests. Success: example can call tools locally and handle tool failures gracefully.
- Structured-output tutorial: start with permissive parsing (attempt to parse JSON from text), then show strong schema contract via typed frames and validation layer. Success: demo shows auto-fix suggestions for minor schema drift.
- Production checklist: steps to harden (schema pinning, canary routing, caching hints).

B) SDK primitives and ergonomics (API surface):
- builder.onPartial(fn) — invoked for each streaming frame; default no-op. Should receive a typed frame wrapper that indicates kind: {text, patch, tool_call, schema_frame}. (Note: this is an API sketch; exact param docs in SDK PR).
- builder.withLatencyBudget(ms) — instructs client and server runtime to prefer lower-latency code-paths (smaller batches, shorter lookahead).
- builder.fallbackPolicy({when: "latency|tool_error|schema_failure", downgrade: "non_streaming|shorter_output|null_tool"}) — declarative fallback rules. Defaults: on tool_error -> return placeholder and continue; on latency -> switch to compact mode.
- sdk.validateSchema(schema, {mode: "warn|strict|auto_fix"}) — lightweight client-side guard. Auto_fix attempts shallow repairs (e.g., wrap bare text in {text: ...}) and surfaces a validation trace to telemetry.

C) Server-side handling and contract points:
- A new header X-Redwood-Latency-Budget used by SDKs to indicate desired latency envelope. Runtime can respond with a Lateral-Mode hint advising which model/variant or whether streaming will be partial.
- Structured frames will include a small envelope field "frame_type" to allow quick client routing without deep parsing.
- Tool-call errors: runtime will emit an idempotent failure frame and continue unless fallbackPolicy instructs to abort.

Telemetry and Observability:
- Developer-visible: sample apps will surface per-call breakdown: client serialization, network RTT, initial-token time, tool-call roundtrip.
- Console logs: clear warnings when fallback triggers (e.g., "fallback: switched to non-streaming due to sustained 95th percentile token latency > 450ms").
- Console-level quick links to Confluence/Jira that describe why the fallback occurred and suggested mitigations (reduce max_tokens_per_request, enable kv-cache).
- Metrics: adoption (how many devs used quickstart -> streaming), fallback rates, time-to-first-success for each ladder rung.

Rollout plan:
- Week 0–2: implement starter templates and streaming example; internal dogfooding by SDK + Docs teams.
- Week 3–5: add fallbackPolicy primitives + server-side header honor; create tool-call sample.
- Week 6–8: structured-output tutorial + schema validation autopatches and telemetry traces.
- Week 9: beta release to selected customers and community repo.

Acceptance criteria:
- Each ladder step has a runnable sample with README and <15 minute onboarding time validated by 3 new engineers outside the team.
- SDK exposes fallbackPolicy and withLatencyBudget; runtime respects X-Redwood-Latency-Budget header in at least two cases (choose model variant / reduce batch size).
- Fall-back events appear in sample app logs with actionable guidance and a corresponding telemetry event in Console.
- Schema validate autopatch successfully repairs > 60% of minor schema drifts in synthetic evals without introducing invalid output.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- How opinionated should default fallback behaviors be? If too aggressive we risk silent quality loss; if too conservative we surface too many errors to novices. Proposed compromise: default to "warn + non-blocking fallback" and require explicit strict mode for production.
- Backwards compatibility for older SDKs that assume raw JSON/strings: we need a compatibility layer in the SDK that can be toggled on.
- Telemetry noise: showing every fallback may overwhelm new users — we should group repeated fallbacks into a single digest after N events.
- Security: tool-call samples may encourage insecure local tooling. We must include a short security section in the starter template warning about executing arbitrary tool outputs.

Prototype notes and TODOs (owner: Avery):
- [ ] Build Node + Python starter templates, prioritizing minimal deps and copy-paste tokens.
- [ ] Add sample web client that visualizes streaming frames and fallback transitions.
- [ ] Draft SDK API surfaces and create a small compatibility layer for older integrations.
- [ ] Wire telemetry traces to Console dev-mode endpoint and assert event shapes.
- [ ] Pair with Docs to create a short 10-minute workshop script for developer on-boarding sessions.

Appendix — quick UX scripts for ladder (for sample README):
- QuickStart (5–10m): create API key -> run example single-call script -> print response.
- Streaming (10–15m): start local dev server, launch web client, see partial tokens populate terminal / browser. Toggle withLatencyBudget(200) and observe different behavior.
- Tool stub (10–20m): run tool stubs, trigger a tool call from model, observe idempotent failure handling by simulator (kill tool stub mid-flight).
- Schema switch (15–25m): run permissive parse, then toggle SDK.validateSchema(..., mode: "strict") and see a validation error and suggested mutation.

Links and references:
- Confluence: CONFLUENCE-1234-hosted-api-onboardings (design notes)
- GitHub: https://github.com/redwood-inference/hosted-sdk/pull/411 (early SDK surface experiment)
- Jira: JIRA-PI-872 (latency-budgeting experiment)

Notes to reviewers:
- Focus review on the ladder sequence and the acceptance criteria. Is there anything missing that would prevent a real developer from reaching a first prototype in under 15 minutes?
- SDK names are provisional. If we accept the ladder concept we should lock new primitives behind a beta flag for 2 releases to minimize churn.

---
Minor style: keep examples terse in starter templates; favor copy-paste success over perfect ergonomics. We can iterate ergonomics after adoption increases.
